questions.question: What is a partition of a bounded interval $I$?
options: An infinite list of real numbers outside $I$.
Finite subintervals covering $I$ with disjoint interiors
A collection of functions defined on $I$.

questions.question: When is a partition called a regular subdivision?
options: When all subintervals have equal length.
When all subintervals contain the number $0$.
When there is only one subinterval.

questions.question: Which collection is a regular subdivision of $[0,1]$?
For the partition $0=x_0<x_1<x_2=1$, which set is one subinterval?
Which relationship between partitions and regular subdivisions is correct?
options: No regular subdivision is a partition.
A regular subdivision must have infinitely many subintervals.
Every regular subdivision is a partition, but not every partition is regular.

questions.question: Why is finiteness part of the definition of a partition here?
options: Because the interval $I$ must contain finitely many points.
Because every subinterval must have length $0$.
Because only finite intervals can contain real numbers.
Because $P_n$ consists of finitely many subintervals indexed by $1\ \le i\ \le n$.

questions.question: A regular subdivision divides $[2,5]$ into $3$ equal subintervals. What is the length of each subinterval?
Which collection is a partition of $[0,1]$ but not a regular subdivision?
Which condition fails if two subintervals of a proposed partition overlap in a point?
options: The condition that $I$ is a bounded interval.
The condition that every $x\in I$ lies in exactly one subinterval.
The condition that subintervals have real endpoints.
The condition that $P_n$ has a name.

questions.question: To approximate an integral by Riemann sums to any desired accuracy, partitions must be refinable. Which guarantee does 'arbitrary fineness' provide?
options: Every partition must have the same number of subintervals.
Every bounded interval has only one possible partition.
One can divide the interval into subintervals that are as small as required.
The interval must be divided into infinitely many subintervals.

questions.question: Why is the collection $[0,\frac{1}{2}]$ and $[\frac{1}{2},1]$ not a partition under the exact wording of this definition?
options: The two subintervals have equal length.
The collection has finitely many intervals.
The point $\frac{1}{2}$ lies in both subintervals.

What must every point of $I$ satisfy in a partition?
options: It must be an endpoint of $I$
It lies in exactly one subinterval
